source_batch.unit_label: BRBL Module B unit 2: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 — Use rebuttable presumptions without treating them as conclusive proof of title or dishonour

facts.statement: Section 118 creates rebuttable presumptions concerning consideration, date, acceptance and transfer timing, indorsement order, stamp on lost instruments and holder-in-due-course status. Its fraud/offence/unlawful-consideration proviso shifts the burden of proving due-course status to the holder. Under section 119, proved protest supports a rebuttable presumption of dishonour.

payload.title: A presumption supplies a starting point, not an unchangeable verdict
payload.core_explanation_md:
Negotiable-instrument disputes do not begin with every fact unproved. **Section 118** supplies presumptions about matters such as consideration, the stated date, timing of acceptance and transfer, and the sequence of indorsements. These operate until contrary evidence is proved.

For a bank preparing a disputed-instrument file, the useful distinction is between a presumption and a conclusion immune from challenge. Preserve documents and transaction evidence even when a statutory presumption initially assists the bank. Do not convert “presumed” into “cannot be disputed”.

self_check.prompt_text: Why should supporting records be preserved even when Section 118 supplies a presumption?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The presumptions can be rebutted by evidence; they are not conclusive proof.

payload.title: Title problems can change who must prove due-course status
payload.core_explanation_md:
The presumption that a holder is a holder in due course has a qualification. Where the instrument was obtained through the offence, fraud or unlawful-consideration circumstances specified in **Section 118(g)**, the holder bears the burden of proving that status. This requires examining the acquisition rather than simply pointing to possession.

**Section 119** deals with a different evidential route: once protest is proved in a suit on a dishonoured instrument, dishonour is presumed unless disproved. It does not turn protest into an answer to every disputed issue, such as title or consideration.

self_check.prompt_text: Does proved protest conclusively settle title to an instrument?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. Section 119 concerns a rebuttable presumption of dishonour, not a general determination of title.

payload.stem_md: A recovery memo says, “The stated date is presumed correct, so no opposing evidence can be considered.” Which revision correctly describes Section 118?

options.text_md: The stated date has no evidential relevance at all
options.explanation_md: Section 118 supplies a date presumption; removing all evidential relevance goes too far.

options.text_md: Only consideration is ever presumed under the Act
options.explanation_md: Section 118 covers several matters, including the date and timing-related presumptions.

options.text_md: The date becomes conclusive once the bank scans the instrument
options.explanation_md: Scanning changes the record medium; it does not convert a rebuttable presumption into conclusive evidence.

options.text_md: The date is a statutory starting presumption that contrary proof can rebut
options.explanation_md: The presumptions apply until the contrary is proved, so the file must allow contrary evidence to be evaluated.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The presumptions apply until the contrary is proved, so the file must allow contrary evidence to be evaluated.

payload.stem_md: In an instrument dispute, the statutory circumstances involving acquisition through fraud under Section 118(g) are established. The holder claims due-course status. Who must prove that status under the proviso?

options.text_md: Nobody, because possession makes the status conclusive
options.explanation_md: The proviso specifically requires proof by the holder in the described circumstances.

options.text_md: The holder claiming to be a holder in due course
options.explanation_md: The fraud/offence/unlawful-consideration proviso places the due-course burden on the holder.

options.text_md: Only the paying banker, regardless of who claims title
options.explanation_md: The proviso identifies the holder, not automatically the paying banker, as bearing this burden.

options.text_md: The clearing house solely because it transmitted an image
options.explanation_md: Image transmission does not allocate the Section 118(g) burden to the clearing house.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The fraud/offence/unlawful-consideration proviso places the due-course burden on the holder.

payload.stem_md: A bank proves protest in a suit on a dishonoured instrument. What is the specific evidential effect under Section 119?

options.text_md: Every prior indorsement becomes genuine beyond challenge
options.explanation_md: Section 119 addresses dishonour; it does not conclusively authenticate every indorsement.

options.text_md: The instrument becomes transferable despite an express prohibition
options.explanation_md: Proof of protest does not override the instrument's transfer restrictions.

options.text_md: Dishonour is presumed unless disproved
options.explanation_md: Section 119 creates this rebuttable presumption once protest is proved.

options.text_md: The holder is awarded the amount without considering any defence
options.explanation_md: A rebuttable presumption is not an automatic final award and does not eliminate all defences.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Section 119 creates this rebuttable presumption once protest is proved.
